topic: Why solid-state drives slow down when they fill up
central_message: The speed of an SSD decreases as it fills up because of how NAND flash memory stores data, specifically due to write amplification and the need for more complex operations when the drive is nearly full.

target_audience.description: General audience with a beginner to intermediate knowledge level in technology. They use apps daily and follow tech news casually but don't fully understand the mechanisms behind technologies.
target_audience.goals: To provide clear mental models they can explain to others, and to convey why they should care about SSD performance.

misconceptions.misconception: SSD speed is not affected by the amount of free space.
misconceptions.correction: SSD performance degrades as it fills up due to factors like write amplification and garbage collection.

misconceptions.misconception: Fragmentation affects SSDs in the same way it does HDDs.
misconceptions.correction: While fragmentation exists in SSDs, it doesn't have the same negative impact as in traditional hard drives because SSDs don't need to physically move data like HDDs do.

misconceptions.misconception: Deleting files on an SSD doesn't free up space effectively.
misconceptions.correction: Deleting files on an SSD frees up space immediately, but the drive's internal processes may still slow down if it's nearly full.

storytelling.approach: Use relatable analogies and scenarios to explain complex technical concepts. For example, comparing NAND flash memory to a library where books (data) are stored in specific sections (cells), and when the library gets crowded, it takes longer to find and replace books.
